title: From Kant to Existentialism: Modern and Contemporary Philosophy

questions.question: Kant's 'Copernican revolution' in philosophy consists in:
options: Asking how objects must conform to our cognition, since the mind supplies the forms of experience
Denying that we can know anything
Proving God's existence
Reducing mind to matter
questions.rationale: Instead of assuming knowledge must copy objects (Hume's problem), Kant argues the mind structures experience with space, time, and the categories — explaining synthetic a priori judgements.

questions.question: For Kant, the things-in-themselves, thinkable but never knowable, are called:
options: Phenomena
Monads
Noumena
The Forms
questions.rationale: Phenomena are things as structured by our cognition; noumena are things as they are apart from knowers — beyond experience.

questions.question: Which of these expresses a formulation of Kant's categorical imperative?
options: Seek the greatest happiness of the greatest number
Act only on maxims you can will as universal law
Follow the command of God
Cultivate your excellence
questions.rationale: Kant gives two leading formulas: universalize your maxim, and treat humanity never merely as a means but always as an end.

questions.question: Hegel's master–slave dialectic shows that:
options: Slavery is a natural institution
History has no direction
The master is fully self-sufficient
Genuine self-consciousness requires mutual recognition between equals
questions.rationale: The master's recognition from an unfree slave is worthless — domination undermines itself. Hegel's dialectic (abstract-negative-concrete, popularly thesis-antithesis-synthesis) drives the development of Spirit.

questions.question: Marx 'turned Hegel right side up' by claiming that:
options: Material economic structures shape law, religion, and ideas
Spirit rather than matter is primary
History ended with the Prussian state
Religion is the heart of a heartless world only
questions.rationale: Historical materialism: the economic base shapes the ideological superstructure, and history is class struggle — the dialectic applied to matter, not Spirit.

questions.question: Nietzsche's proclamation 'God is dead' means:
options: A literal theological claim
He personally lost his faith as a child
The shared moral horizon grounded in belief in God has collapsed
Atheism should be illegal
questions.rationale: The death of God is a cultural diagnosis: the collapse of the foundation of European values — met with the will to power and perspectivism instead of new consolations.

questions.question: Sartre's formula 'existence precedes essence' asserts that:
options: Human nature is fixed by God
We first exist, then define ourselves through free choices
Essence is an illusion
Only the body is real
questions.rationale: With no pre-given human nature, we are radically free and responsible; fleeing this freedom by hiding in roles is bad faith (Being and Nothingness, 1943).

questions.question: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex (1949) opens its argument with which claim?
options: Women are naturally suited to domestic life
Freedom is an illusion
Gender is purely biological
One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman
questions.rationale: De Beauvoir applies existentialism to gender: femininity is a constructed situation that a situated freedom must navigate.

questions.question: Camus's 'absurd' is best defined as:
options: The claim that life is meaningless so anything is permitted
The clash between our demand for meaning and the universe's silence
A logical contradiction in Hegel
The impossibility of knowledge
questions.rationale: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) answers the absurd not with suicide but with revolt, freedom, and passion — one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

questions.question: Popper's criterion of demarcation holds that a theory is scientific only if:
options: It is confirmed by every observation
It can in principle be falsified by a failed prediction
A majority of scientists accept it
It fits within the ruling paradigm
questions.rationale: For Popper, falsifiability separates science from non-science; science grows by conjectures and refutations. Kuhn, by contrast, described paradigm-governed normal science and revolutionary shifts.
